sections.html:
Twiggs County calls itself the geographic center of Georgia. Jeffersonville is the county seat. The north end rolls like the Piedmont, while the south has the flat pine woods of south Georgia, and kaolin, forestry and farming have long driven the economy. Interstate 16 runs through the middle, linking Macon and Savannah, and two industrial parks of 150 and 500 acres sit where I-16 meets Highway 96.

Nearly nine in ten Twiggs homes, 88.2%, house their owners, and the middle value is $111,300. People are leaving more than arriving: the 2025 estimate of 7,597 sits 5.4% under the 2020 base of 8,028. Builders pulled just 13 permits in 2025, and 96.1% of residents had not moved in the prior year. The county averages 22.3 people per square mile, so many parcels are acreage, timber or family land handed down. A seller with that kind of property often values a quick as-is closing over weeks of showings.

Many owners have little cash set aside for repairs or back taxes. A seller in that position can ask the tax commissioner early what payoff will come out of the proceeds and weigh an as-is sale against fixing the house first.

The courthouse at 425 Railroad Street in Jeffersonville holds the offices you need, and each has its own job.

  • Tax commissioner, (478) 945-3359, mail to P.O. Box 187: property and motor vehicle tax, tags and titles.
  • Assessors and Chief Appraiser, Room 102, (478) 945-3663, mail to P.O. Box 111: values, returns, homestead, current-use and forest land programs, and appeals.
  • County commissioners: adopt the budget and help set the county millage.

The assessors' board gathers on the first Thursday of every month in Room 102, starting at nine in the morning, and the office accepts walk-in filings during the nine-to-five business day. A field appraiser with photo identification in a marked county vehicle may stop by a parcel to check data tied to an appeal, return, permit or sale.

Go by the date on your own statement. The Georgia default is December 20, but a county can choose December 1 or November 15 or bill in installments, which makes the Twiggs tax commissioner the final word on yours.

Interest cannot start until 60 days after the bill's postmark, and unpaid balances may add penalties on top. Phone (478) 945-3359 for the exact date, the current interest rate and a payoff on any past-due year. Mobile home owners should ask separately, since the permit and return follow their own early-year cycle.

  • A refund claim for tax wrongly assessed must start within three years after you paid.
  • In some counties the city clerk bills municipal tax, so confirm whether a Jeffersonville or other city bill applies to your parcel.

Notices of assessment are mailed in late May or early June, and the deadline is 45 days after the printed date. A plain letter works as well as the form if it lists the parcel ID, address, daytime phone, your chosen route and your evidence. Hand-delivered or postmarked papers count. Late filings are not processed, and the office refuses email and fax.

You pick one of three routes when you file:

  • Board of Equalization: free, with three local property owners who each completed at least 40 hours of training. Either party has 30 days to carry the result to Superior Court.
  • Nonbinding arbitration: you provide a certified appraisal dated no more than nine months before January 1, plus a $214 check to the Clerk of Superior Court. If the county accepts your appraisal, the fee comes back.
  • Hearing officer: for value or uniformity disputes over non-homestead property or wireless personal property above $500,000, at no filing cost.

Timing differs by route. On the hearing officer path, the assessors have up to 90 days to review and answer, you then have 30 days to say you are unhappy, and the assessors have another 30 days to send the file to the appeal administrator. If no hearing officer is found, the appeal moves to the Board of Equalization. Either side may ask for the other's witness list and documents at least 10 days before a hearing, and the answer is due at least seven days ahead, or the evidence can be excluded.

File in Room 102 with the assessors before April 1 of the first year you want relief. The home must be your primary residence, and a missed deadline counts as a waiver for that year.

The assessors also administer the Conservation Use Valuation Assessment and Forest Land Protection Act programs, which matter in a county where farms and timber dominate. These programs carry covenants, so ask for the commitment length before you enroll land you plan to sell soon. For current exemption amounts, call (478) 945-3663.

Most Twiggs County parcels are acreage or long-held family property, so a little preparation goes a long way.

  1. Call the tax commissioner for a written balance on each year still open.
  2. Ask the assessors whether the land is enrolled in a conservation or forest program and what the covenant requires of the next owner.
  3. Confirm your homestead is on file if you live in the house.
  4. Pull the parcel ID from your last bill so each office can find the record at once.
  5. Pass every written figure to the closing agent before you accept an offer.

Doing this in advance means no tax surprise slows the closing, and you know what will come out of your proceeds.

Obtain a payoff in writing from the tax commissioner and compare it to the settlement statement. Because Georgia bills the January 1 title holder, a sale late in the year needs the tax divided clearly on paper.

If you inherited land, ask for the history of every year you or the estate held it, since acreage in a shrinking county sometimes sits unpaid longer than a house in town. A bill unpaid more than 90 days after its due date can become a lien filed with the Clerk of Superior Court. Settling past years at closing clears the title for a buyer, whether that buyer finances or pays cash.

Bring the parcel ID and a copy of your deed when you visit the courthouse, and ask each office for its figures in writing. A cash buyer can close without a lender's appraisal or repair demands, which helps when family land has outbuildings or timber that a loan underwriter might question.

faqs.q: How do I reach the Twiggs County tax commissioner?
faqs.a: Call (478) 945-3359 or visit the Court House Square at 425 Railroad Street in Jeffersonville. Mail goes to P.O. Box 187.

faqs.q: How long can I appeal a Twiggs County value?
faqs.a: Forty-five days after the notice date. Papers must be hand-delivered or postmarked by then, and neither email nor fax appeals are accepted.

faqs.q: Does Twiggs County offer arbitration for appeals?
faqs.a: Yes. Nonbinding arbitration needs a certified appraisal and a $214 filing fee, and either side can later appeal the arbitrator's decision to Superior Court.

faqs.q: What is the homestead cutoff in Twiggs County?
faqs.a: April 1 of the first year you want it. Apply at the assessors' Room 102 in the courthouse.

faqs.q: Why does Twiggs County have so few building permits?
faqs.a: Only 13 permits were issued in 2025 in a county of about 7,600 people. The county is rural, and population has fallen since 2020.
